title: Real interest rate vs. nominal interest rate
subtitle: The Fisher Equation and the real purchasing power of an interest rate
openingQuestion: The bank rate is 8%, inflation is 6%. What is the real interest rate?
openingOptions: 14%, from adding the inflation on top of the bank rate
explanation: The nominal interest rate is the number the bank publishes; the real interest rate is what's left after subtracting inflation, i.e. the actual increase in purchasing power. Distinguishing the two matters because every economic decision reacts to the real rate: depositing savings at 8% when inflation is 6% only makes you about 2% richer. When the real rate turns negative, holding cash is a guaranteed loss of purchasing power, and that's when capital flows heavily into assets instead.

realWorldExample.description: When inflation in Vietnam rises during certain periods, bank savings rates that appear attractive in nominal terms (7-8%/year) actually deliver a very low or even negative real interest rate after subtracting inflation - causing savers to lose purchasing power even as their account balance keeps growing in numbers.

quiz.question: How do TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities) protect investors?
options: The nominal rate is always higher than a regular Treasury bond
The coupon rate adjusts with CPI, the face value stays the same
The original principal is adjusted upward with CPI
The interest income is exempt from federal income tax
quiz.explanation: TIPS: principal rises with CPI. If CPI rises 5%, the principal rises 5% → coupon (%) × principal is larger → real income is preserved. Investors worried about inflation often choose TIPS despite a lower nominal yield.

quiz.question: If the State Bank announces the nominal savings rate rising from 6% to 8%, but inflation also rises from 3% to 7% at the same time, is the saver actually better off?
options: No change - both rose together so the real rate stays at 3%
Yes - the real rate rises by 2 points, exactly matching the nominal increase
Yes - the real rate rises from 3% to 8% because inflation isn't subtracted
No - the real rate falls from 3% (6%-3%) down to 1%
quiz.explanation: This is the core lesson of the Fisher Equation: looking only at the nominal rate while ignoring inflation can lead to a completely wrong conclusion about whether you're actually 'better off' - the real rate (adjusted for inflation) is the accurate measure of the actual increase in purchasing power.

quiz.question: The nominal rate is 9%, inflation is 4%. What is the approximate real interest rate?
options: About 5% (= 9% - 4%, a quick estimate)
About 13% (= 9% + 4%, adding inflation on top)
About 2.25% (= 9% ÷ 4%, dividing the two figures)
About 36% (= 9% × 4%, multiplying the two figures)
quiz.explanation: The quick estimate is the difference: 9% - 4% = 5%. The exact Fisher formula gives 4.81%, so subtraction is good enough when inflation is moderate.

quiz.question: What does a negative real interest rate mean for a saver?
options: The bank charges a fee instead of paying interest on deposits
The balance grows, but it buys fewer goods than last year
The account balance gradually shrinks month by month
The deposit is taxed more heavily than the interest received
quiz.explanation: Depositing 100 million at 4% becomes 104 million, but 7% inflation means the same old basket of goods now costs 107 million. The account looks prettier while purchasing power gets poorer - this is why you must always look at the real rate.

quiz.question: Why do borrowers benefit when inflation unexpectedly rises?
options: Because inflation reduces the total balance recorded on the books
Because the loan's interest rate automatically falls as inflation rises
Because they repay a fixed debt with money that has lost value
Because banks are forced to restructure debt once inflation exceeds a threshold
quiz.explanation: The obligation to repay 1 billion in five years is fixed, but 1 billion then buys less than it does today. Unexpected inflation transfers value from creditor to debtor - which is why creditors demand an inflation premium upfront.

keyTakeaways: Negative real rate: money in the bank loses purchasing power

practicePrompt.question: You deposit savings at a nominal rate of 7%/year, while that year's inflation is 5%. Does the real purchasing power of your money grow by exactly 7%, or actually less?
options: Yes, purchasing power grows by exactly 7% because the bank rate already reflects every economic factor
No - the real rate = 7% - 5% = 2%, and this is the true increase in purchasing power
Purchasing power grows by more than 7% because compounding amplifies the cumulative effect further
Inflation has no effect on the purchasing power of a fixed-rate savings deposit
practicePrompt.explanation: Real rate ≈ Nominal rate - Inflation = 7% - 5% = 2%. The nominal rate is the number the bank publishes, but the real rate is what accurately reflects the increase in purchasing power after subtracting what inflation 'erodes' - an important consideration when evaluating long-term investment performance.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a definition to recite rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.

application.title: Calculate your own real interest rate
application.message: Take the bank savings rate you currently have, subtract the current inflation rate to get the real rate - see whether your deposit is actually growing your purchasing power.
application.secondary: Many people are surprised to find their real rate is close to zero or negative.

sections.text: An 8% savings rate sounds attractive - but if that year's inflation is also 6%, the real increase in your purchasing power is only about 2%. This is exactly the gap between the nominal rate - the number the bank publishes - and the real rate - the actual increase in purchasing power after subtracting inflation.
The Fisher Equation: the formula linking the two rates

The exact formula is (1 + r_real) = (1 + r_nominal) / (1 + inflation), but with moderate inflation, people usually use the approximation: r_real ≈ r_nominal - inflation. For example, a nominal rate of 8% and inflation of 6% → real rate ≈ 2%. If inflation spikes up to exactly match the nominal rate, the real rate falls to zero - your bank deposit generates no real return at all, even though the account balance keeps rising steadily.

To protect investors from unexpected inflation risk, the US government issues TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities): the face value of TIPS is adjusted upward with CPI. If CPI rises 5% in a year, the TIPS face value also rises 5%, causing the coupon payment (calculated as a % of the new face value) to rise along with it, preserving real income for the investor - even though TIPS' nominal yield is usually lower than a regular bond of the same term.

items: Nominal rate: the number published in the contract, before subtracting inflation
Real rate: the actual growth in purchasing power, more important for evaluating an investment
A negative real rate (inflation > nominal rate): saving money = losing purchasing power over time
TIPS and other CPI-anchored instruments: a direct way to protect against inflation risk

sections.label: The Vietnam lesson
sections.text: When inflation in Vietnam rises high, a 7-8%/year savings rate sounds attractive but may only deliver a very low or negative real rate - always check the gap against inflation before concluding that a rate is 'good'.
